name: Jamal Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential; you can tell me what you say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead a claims team at Fern Insurance, mostly storm and repair cases. I use our approved AI assistant every day to sort photos and draft letters, then I check dates, exclusions and the payment before anything goes out. I have a bachelor's degree and earn well for a clerk, but I still sign my name to the decision.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What stays with you after a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a small place alone and have eleven months of expenses in an emergency account, separate from a house fund. There are several insurers within a train ride. A wrong date on a claim bothers me more than an untidy desk, because somebody might lose a payment over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AI Plateau describes what we already see: quick drafts, plenty of mistakes and people still owning the claim. I use the approved assistant each day to sort storm photos, then check every line before a payment letter leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the small time saving. I lead the claims desk, earn well for the job and have eleven months of expenses saved, so I don't see my own wage threatened by a tool that still misses dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep clearing the claims queue and show two newer clerks the three checks I use on every AI draft. I'll put 250 from each monthly pay cheque into my house fund and keep the final sign-off under my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'm more annoyed by the old printer than by this version of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake did the tool make last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool once moved a repair date from March to May because it read the upload time. A machine moved the repair date by two months, and my eyes kept a customer from losing a claim. Now the two new clerks check dates first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your savings plan pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I rent alone, and the house fund is a choice rather than a rescue pot. I would still save the 250, because the ordinary cost of moving is real even if AI levels off.

say: I'd call **AI Plateau** useful for drafts but still prone to mistakes.
I'd keep a clerk's **final sign-off** on every payment letter.
think: My **senior wage** looks secure when the tool still misses claim dates.
I have eleven months saved and **room to choose** a house plan.
do: Keep **clearing storm claims** and teach two newer clerks my three checks on every draft.
Save **250 monthly** into the house fund.
S0.quote: A machine moved the repair date by two months, and my eyes kept a customer from losing a claim.
fieldNote: He uses the **approved assistant daily** but checks its work himself.
His senior wage and **eleven-month reserve** support a calm outlook.
Savings serve a **house purchase**, not an immediate job crisis.

steps.text: Keep checking AI claim drafts and coach two new clerks on dates
Move 250 monthly from claims wages to house savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption makes machine drafts common and pushes the insurer to raise targets. The thinking work changes now; robots for physical inspections arrive more slowly, and our office has few physical tasks anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use the tools better than most people on my team, but that could mean one lead checking work that three clerks used to do. My salary may hold while bonus hours vanish, so I need to watch the actual payslip rather than claim I'm safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask my manager for a paid eight-week trial of the new claims assistant with a log of wrong decisions. I'll keep doing final reviews and check the advertised fraud-review roles nearby; I would move only if the net pay after train costs covers my rent and house savings target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing bonus hours, though my base wage looks sound for now. I can run the error trial and compare written offers before choosing another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count wrong refusals, not just minutes saved. If the insurer removes a reviewer, I want the audit log to show who is responsible for a bad payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell family about another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A higher title can come with fewer paid hours. I'd tell my sister Amira that much. I can afford to wait for a written offer with real hours, and I would not pretend a job advert is a signed contract.

say: I'd demand a **wrong-decision log** before raising claims targets.
I'd say **thinking tasks** change before slower robots reach inspections.
think: I could lose **bonus hours** even if my base wage stays.
I may be left **checking three clerks' work** alone on a leaner team.
do: Run an **eight-week paid trial** and log wrong claim decisions.
Keep **final claim reviews** while checking posted fraud roles.
Compare **net pay after trains** with rent before any move.
feel: **Anxious** about losing my own bonus pay, with base wages intact for now.
S1.quote: A higher title can come with fewer paid hours.
fieldNote: Daily AI use does not erase his concern about **paid bonus hours**.
He wants **wrong refusals measured**, not only time saved.
A job switch requires a **written offer**.

steps.text: Keep final claim reviews and log errors in an eight-week paid trial
Check paid fraud-review vacancies and compare net pay after train fare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch AGI by 2028 could check nearly every claim and write every letter before capable robots arrive around 2031. We owe customers an appeal route and staff a real account of which posts will be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead role could go when thinking AI is cheaper than a claims team. Eleven months of savings and a few insurers nearby let me search, but I cannot bank on fraud review staying human or my house fund surviving a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask for the redundancy terms and put my rent, insurance and food into one monthly figure. I'll stop the house deposit transfer for now, move 350 a month from current wages into emergency savings and apply for posted paid dispute roles, checking net pay after transport and confirmed hours before accepting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own wage, but not lost. I have months to search and I can make the budget today; I am not awake at night without a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens the month after a job cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month after a cut I'd claim the support I'm entitled to and pay rent from the reserve. I wouldn't buy a fraud certificate until someone confirms the fee, paid study time and an actual vacancy that my qualification meets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a fraud certificate open a safe path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bachelor's degree and claims experience may get an interview, not a wage. I would ask what checks the disputes job legally requires and whether the insurer will fund them before I spend the house money. My degree may get an interview, but an interview does not pay the rent.

say: I'd demand **paid-post plans** and a human claim appeal route.
I'd explain **2028 thinking AI** arrives before robots around 2031.
think: My **lead post could go**, despite daily AI skill.
I have eleven months saved, but **fraud roles may shrink** too.
do: Get **redundancy terms** and list fixed monthly bills.
Pause **house-deposit transfers** and save 350 monthly for emergencies.
Apply for **paid disputes roles** only when net pay and hours work.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible lost wage, with a budget and time.
S2.quote: My degree may get an interview, but an interview does not pay the rent.
fieldNote: He expects possible **personal job loss** but describes control and ordinary sleep.
His house fund becomes an **emergency reserve** under the fast scenario.

steps.text: Get redundancy terms and check eligible income support after a cut
Save 350 monthly from current claims wages for emergencies
Apply for paid disputes roles if net pay and confirmed hours cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us five years to prove where a human appeal is needed. Robots around 2034 come later, but my screen work faces the thinking change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use those years to learn claim auditing and build the house fund while I still earn well. I cannot assume an audit title survives full AGI, so I would test the paid market before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll take the insurer's funded audit course during paid hours if it meets the regulator's qualification rule. I'll build a sample of twenty disputed claims, save 300 monthly and compare advertised audit jobs after train costs with rent. In the first year after 2031, I'd keep my paid role if it exists and move only for a written audit offer with enough net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether my claims desk or a paid audit post will exist by 2031. The five years let me train while earning and check the real vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the course teaches the right rules?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the audit lead to review five of my sample cases and tell me where I missed a rule. If the course is just a badge the insurer invented, I won't spend paid hours on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep your current job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira would ask why I don't quit now while my savings are strong. My current pay funds both the house and a safer change. A five-year warning is valuable only while the wages keep coming.

say: I'd ask for **qualified, paid audit training** before AGI reaches claims in 2031.
I'd note **2034 robots** follow the change to screen work.
think: I can build **audit skill and savings** while earning well.
I cannot assume an **audit title survives AGI** or keeps my wage.
do: Take **funded audit training** if it meets qualification rules.
Build a **twenty-claim sample** for the audit lead to review.
Save **300 monthly** and compare written audit offers after train costs.
feel: **Anxious** about my future wage, with time to train while employed.
S3.quote: My current pay funds both the house and a safer change.
fieldNote: He makes training conditional on a **real regulator qualification** and paid hours.
The five-year horizon supports **testing claims work**, not an immediate resignation.
A switch still needs **enough net pay**.

steps.text: Take funded regulator-qualifying audit course during paid hours
Build twenty disputed-claim sample and ask audit lead to review five cases
Save 300 monthly from current claims wages
Compare written audit offers after train fare with rent before moving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 leaves ten years to build fair appeals and train staff who check them. Robots around 2039 may inspect physical damage, but policy reading and customer letters change earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep a good wage through most of the decade and have the house deposit ready long before then. Still, I would not call a future claims role guaranteed just because I am the person who uses AI every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading claims this year, save 300 monthly for the house and audit one AI claim sample each week. Every birthday I'll compare posted paid audit roles with my current pay; in the first year after 2036, I'll stay in a paid role if there is one or take a written offer that covers rent after travel costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. A ten-year date lets me keep a normal life while I check the numbers each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check at the first birthday review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the first birthday review I'll count the house deposit and ask whether claim audits still need a named person. If the jobs have changed, I can adjust the plan without leaving paid work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Amira I still plan to buy a place if the numbers work. A decade is long enough for a house plan, but I would keep the emergency reserve separate.

say: I'd use the **decade to 2036** for house savings and fair claims checks.
I'd say **robots around 2039** follow the earlier desk-work change.
think: I may keep **good wages** while building a house deposit.
My daily AI use does not **guarantee future paid work**.
do: Keep **leading claims** and audit one AI sample weekly.
Save **300 monthly** toward the house, apart from emergencies.
Compare **paid audit vacancies** with my current net wage each birthday.
feel: **Calm** about near-term pay, with yearly checks.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough for a house plan, but I would keep the emergency reserve separate.
fieldNote: He keeps **house savings separate** from the eleven-month emergency reserve.
Daily tool use supports current work but does not prove **future job safety**.
The post-2036 route depends on **written paid hours**.

steps.text: Keep leading claims and audit one AI claim sample weekly
Save 300 monthly toward the house apart from emergency money

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose even the lead post I built around checking tools. Clear redundancy terms, eligible income support and a funded route to a regulator-qualified paid audit job would help me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a fraud or audit certificate actually qualifies someone for the vacancy. My degree may get an interview, but an interview does not pay the rent.

headlineQuote: Ask whether a fraud or audit certificate actually qualifies someone for the vacancy.
portrait: Jamal leads **storm claims** at Fern and uses approved AI every day with manual checks.
His **eleven-month reserve** and high wage give him room to test options; he rents alone.
Steady change could trim **bonus hours**, while fast AGI could remove his lead post.
He wants **regulator-qualified training**, written paid offers and net wages that cover rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could replace his lead claims post despite his daily tool skill.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written terms**, income help and funded regulator-qualified training tied to a paid vacancy.
